speechtext: Might I ask was not that report of the War Office-the so-called report of the War Office-brought before the Public Accounts Committee nearly a year ago ?

It was before that committee from the 15th of March, 1907. In a debate which took place in this House on January 14, 1907, I made the following statement:
In addition to that, the Ross rifle had been subjected ito the severest test by a committee of the War Office in England.
When?

Recently, and the report is most satisfactory from the point of view of the military experts here. They found the same defects which had been discovered here, though not all of them, and all the defects which they discovered had been remedied before this report reached us.
I simply quote this to show that I had actually mentioned the fact that there was such a report, some weeks before the papers were laid on the table, thus showing no desire whatever on my part to cover up in any way this particular report.

I would like to ask tlie hon. minister if it is his intention to give the impression to this House that the rifles pronounced upon by the Royal School of Musketry at Hythe were not submitted by the Militia Department or the Ross Rifle factory ? If not, has the hon. minister any means of explaining how any rifles came to be pronounced upon and if the report signed by Mr. Broderick, Lord Middleton, then Secretary of State for War, did not say that two Ross rifles had been examined by the officers of Musketry School at Hythe, in comparison with two Lee-En-field rifles, and that the result was marked inferiority of the Ross rifle

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This matter has come up as a question of privilege and cannot be allowed to drift into a discussion. All the hon. gentleman is entitled to do is ask a question.
I shall be very happy to answer the question.
I want to ask another ?
One at a time. Perhaps better let me answer the first.

It is about the same subject. Take the report from the Woolwich Arsenal, I would like to ask the minister if he considers that a favourable report. He said it was considered favourable by the military experts in this country. If it be a favourable report, I would like to ask who are the experts that pronounced upon it.

I read my statement which I made in the House last session and which speaks for itself. In that statement I said that the report was considered favourable, inasmuch as all the faults or defects mentioned in that report had been remedied before the report reached us. With regard to the alleged test in 1902, that is an entirely different tiling. The Woolwich test took place in 1906. I think the Hythe alleged test took place in 1902, and I have already said that no Ross rifles were sent by the government nor by Sir Charles Ross nor by anybody on his behalf to Hythe, much less to be tested at Hythe.

Mr. Speaker, in the discussion of a measure dealing with the franchise of the people of this country it is rather unfortunate that so much heat and party bias should be shown. It is equally unfortunate that in the year 1908 we have not yet a perfect franchise Act upon our statute-book and that we find it necessary from time to time to make amendments that will meet complaints and remedy the evils that do exist. But, we can find consolation in the fact that in the mother of parliaments, up to 1832, they had no franchise that was worthy of the name,

The point I particularly wish to emphasize is that the imperial government does not accept these lists without the right of appeal, nor would they accept provincial lists without the right of appeal had they provinces in Great Britain. In Canada we had our changing systems of registration and franchise. Provincial lists were first accepted
__accepted but not without complaints and
objections such as we hear in this House to-day, and these complaints came from our Conservative friends. They complained that in Nova Scotia a Franchise Act was passed which treated Conservatives unfairly in the then approaching federal election and that when this measure accomplished its object it was repealed before the next provincial election. They complained of an unfair franchise in Prince Edward Island, and so far as the Conservative party was concerned they complained wherever there was a Liberal* government in power in any of the provinces. They always complained that they were being defrauded in the preparation of the lists by the party opposed to them in politics who had control of the provincial government. It is not pertinent to this debate to discuss the merits or demerits of these claims, but it surely must be accepted by both sides of the House as sound policy that a man properly qualified and anxious to vote in a federal election has the undoubted right to look to this parliament for redress of any grievance real or imaginary, and not to anybody over which this parliament has no control. Our Conservative friends passed the Dominion Franchise Act tn 1885 and the last state

was worse than the first; not so much because of the violation of any correct principle but because of the cumbersome, expensive, and dishonest machinery provided to carry the legislation into effect. This legislation proved so unsatisfactory that some even of our Conservative friends wanted it repealed, and in 1884, Sir John Thompson who then led the House made an honest effort to repeal the existing law, but the influences within his party were so strong that the Bill was not passed. The House refused to accept a similar Bill introduced by Mr. Charlton in 1895, and the Conservative party went out of power in 1896 with the Dominion Franchise Act providing for Dominion lists on the statute-book. Under the Conservative Franchise Act, revision was so expensive that it was seldom attempted and sometimes elections were held on lists over two years old so that a man had to be twenty-three years of age before he could exercise his franchise in Canada. During the .time the Act was in force four revisions cost nearly $2,000,000 to this country. Revising barristers were political partisans of the worst description and the record shows that even Conservatives were heartily sick of the legislation. I am bound to say-because I was not in the House in 1898-that the Liberal party went to the other extreme in their legislation of that year. They accepted provincial lists with practically no conditions attached except that the then Solicitor General sounded a note of caution in reference to these lists. I find in ' Hansard ' page 3952 (1898) that the 'Solicitor General made this statement:

But let me give you a particular gem from the hon. member. He is complaining of our not accepting the Manitoba lists at the present time. Here is the opinion he had of the provincial lists in 1898:
However, I see by the provision of this Bill the Northwest Territories are exempted from its operation and now I ask the government to (place Manitoba in the same category as the Northwest Territories, at least until such time as they can bring pressure to bear on their Liberal confreres of Manitoba to get them to wipe off the statutes of that province an Act that is now a disgrace to it, and for it, substitute a fair Act; a Franchise Act in the widest and truest sense of the term; an Act that will give ia Conservative in that province an equal say in its affairs with his Liberal fellowman.
This was the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Marquette in 1898. But he is quite satisfied now to reverse that opinion and accept the Provincial Act. When the men, for whom he is the chief apologist in this House, is in power in Manitoba, he is quite prepared to accept for himself and party the political advantages to be gained through the rascality of his rascally officials in Manitoba. When, however, there was a Liberal government in office in that province in 1898, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) was the man who howled the loudest because this parliament was going to revert to the provincial lists.
We have another charming gentleman in the House, and I am sorry he is not here to-day, because I want to say kind words about him. I refer to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). We. love him for his inconsistency. I think he is making a serious mistake when he devotes his time to politics at all. He ought to devote his entire time to the practice of law, because whether he be right or wrong he is equally at home in the discussion of an argument. We always admire his facility and felicity of expression and the cogency of his argument, whether he is on the right or the wrong side. Why, in 1898, he was the fighting lieutenant from the province of Quebec for the valiant Sir Charles Tupper. He was not satisfied then with protesting against reverting to the provincial lists, but was the bold had man who introduced an amendment for the purpose of doing in 1898 what is proposed to be done in the legislation now introduced. Let me quote from his speech, page 4056 from ' Hansard ' :
But this much I do contend, that it was intended by the framers of our constitution that as soon as possible after confederation, with a view of welding the people together with a view of making one people of all those who inhabited British North America, we Mr. D. ROSS.
should control our own franchise, establish exactly how it should be exercised and not relinquish that franchise to the provinces, thus producing conditions of inequality, as we are now doing by this Bill.
This is the gentleman who the other day threatened to obstruct Supply and put the civil servants on bread and water. Why? Because the government is doing in 1908 what he advised the government to do in 1898. Consistency is a precious and rare jewel but it never gets within hailing distance of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).
Then comes the noblest Tory of them all, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). He had some very strnog views in the Franchise Act in 1898. No doubt he has strong views to-day because in 1898 he told us that:
So long as I have a seat in this parliament I will contend that it is essentially necessary for the dignity and best government of Canada as a nation, that she shall have uninterrupted- and absolute coutrol of her own franchise. And I believe that the great majority of the people of this country will not be satisfied to have it otherwise.
Again he said :
I think the government would have done a useful thing for this country, and would have kept its position and that of its supporters logical and consistent, and would have made itself square with public opinion if it had allowed- the plea of the opposition which is simply that in the last resort, the voters' lists shall be subject to the revision of a competent court of law.
I am bound to say that we on this side have exercised due caution in accepting the advice of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), but no doubt he will be extremely flattered to find that after ten long years of consideration we have practically determined to accept his advice. The hon. gentleman said :
So long as I have a seat in this parliament I will contend that it is essentially necessary for the dignity and best government of Canada that she should have uninterrupted and absolute control of her own franchise
The hon. gentleman did not always have a seat in parliament since then. There was an unfortunate hiatus, but no doubt this will in no way influence him in his opinion with reference to a proper Franchise,. Act. He told us some three years ago that, disappointed in politics, he had changed his views somewhat with reference to the education question, but I am sure that the fact that he did not always have a seat in parliament is not going to make him change his views with reference to the Franchise Act, and I feel quite confident that, in accordance with those views, we shall find him voting for the measure now introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth).

These extracts I have quoted show the position which these hon. gentlemen took in 1898. I am not going to quarrel with that position. I believe it was a strong position. I believe that while it is convenient to accept provincial lists, this parliament should not, under any circumstances, divest itself of all responsibility to see that people who are entitled to vote in federal elections should be given the opportunity of voting.
Where does the leader of the opposition stand to-day on this question ? In 1898 he did not take so prominent a part in the discussion of public affairs as he does to-day, but he was then a member of this House, and he then pleaded for a court of appeal, particularly in his own province of Nova Scotia. He said that his Conservative friends were not likely to get justice down there, and he wanted a court of appeal. I say again tjiere is nothing in the legislation we are now discussing which has anything else for object than the putting of people on the list who are entitled to be there and taking people off who should not be there. That is the only object of the measure. My hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, cannot very well escape from the position which he and his party have taken in connection with this question. He also threatened obstruction. Why ? Because parliament, after ten years experience, is adopting a measure which has for its object the relief of those who think they have been unfairly dealt with by the provincial officials. He is in favour of the disfranchisement of those entitled to exercise their franchise in federal matters and of enfranchisement ignorant foreigners, made British subjects by fraudulent naturalization papers. He turns a deaf ear to the appeals of those who expect relief from this parliament from the acts of dishonest officials, acting in the interests of partisan government, and is going to stand for such a list to the point of -political exhaustion.
Why does he want such a list ? Why is he opposed to an honest list in a Dominion election ? Is it because he cannot hope for success on any other list than such a list as we have in Manitoba to-day ? We say, Sir, that the time has come *when a large body of voters in this country claim that abuses have crept into the system of administration in Manitoba ; and whether these charges are or are not well founded It is the bounden duty of this government and this parliament to say to those people that in so far as their franchise in federal matters is concerned, any doubts are to be removed. Can it be said that John Smith, an intelligent Canadian, a desirable citizen, a payer of taxes, who takes a keen and intelligent interest in the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, in the all red route, in the tariff, in immigration matters, in all questions of a purely federal character, who travels from his home a distance of
100 miles to the office of the registration clerk in his provincial registration district and finds that there are so many people ahead of him that the clerk has no time to take his application, and his name therefore cannot go on the list and also finds that there are others whose names go on the list by fraud-shall it be said that this man is not to get his undoubted right to exercise his franchise in federal elections ? Shall it be said that John Smith is to be left to the loving kindness and tender mercies of Bob. Rogers. This government has no control over the government of Manitoba or any other provincial government-
How is that for a point of order Mr. Speaker, are governments to be spoken of in that slighting way ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The reference was to a member of a provincial government. I am inclined to think the rule does not apply to members of a provincial government.
It is a question of taste on the part of the member speaking.

I do not think the hon. gentleman has taken his point of order very seriously. This parliament has no control over the government of Manitoba or any other provincial government in the matter of making whatever provision it deems best for the granting of the franchise for provincial elections. Provincial governments can give the people, for provincial purposes, what franchise they see fit ; but this parliament has the right and it is its bounden duty to see that every man properly qualified is protected in liis right to vote in a federal election. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Bake) who is not in the House, became rather alarmed the other evening. He sounded a note of warning to the premier that there was likely to be trouble, even bloodshed, if this legislation was passed and there was any attempt to dishonestly disfranchise the electors. I reiterate that warning. There always should be trouble if the electors are dishonestly disfranchised. As I said before there is not one single provision in this Bill which has for its object the disfranchisement of any one, and it is up to the government to see that the officials appointed under this legislation do their work honestly. Generally speaking the people of tlie west, whether Liberal or Conservative, want honest voters' lists and honest elections and they will. stand for no other kind. But I want to sound another note of warning to the right hon. the Prime Minister and it is that the people of Manitoba, of British Columbia or of any other western province can be left to take care of any one in office there who tampers with voters' lists who gives dishonest voters' lists ; but they will

not submit to this parliament allowing such officials to disfranchise them for federal elections and they expect this parliament to protect them in their federal franchise, without any regard for the opinions of any provincial authority.
What are the complaints against the existing system ? The voters' lists in Manitoba to-day is five years old. It has been continued from year to year by Acts of the provincial legislature, with the result that it is loaded up with dead men, absentees and people without fixed residence. The courts of revision in Manitoba are constituted and organized to obstruct the proper purging of the voters' lists. The revising judge sits from 1 o'clock to 6 o'clock only. All the time can be taken up in the hearing of the evidence in one case.
That is not so.
My hon. friend says that is not so.
No. You may find an individual case-

Oh, no, it is not so now, because the government of Manitoba and its officials have been making a show of righteousness during the last two or three days that they did not make in the last two or three years.
I make the statement that it never was so.
It is in some cases.
Perhaps in half a dozen cases but it is not by any means the rule.

I am making the statement, I am making it upon the authority of those who know, upon the authority of those in whom I have confidence, that revising barristers have sat from 1 o'clock to 6 o'clock on one day only.

They have.
Mr. I). ROSS. And all that time could be taken up in hearing the evidence in one case.
Can you give an illustration of that having occurred ?
Illustration after illustration.
Give us one.

I have not one at hand, but if the hon. gentleman would read some of the speeches by hon. members for Manitoba-and they would do him a world of good-he would find numerous illustrations of what I am quoting. When six o'clock comes court is over and the other cases remain unheard ; the dead men and the others remain on the list.
It is absolutely uncommon.
Our friends do not like this.
We like the truth.

The additions to the list in Manitoba are made by registration clerks appointed by order in council by the government-who also, by order in council, fix one place in each constituency to receive applications and one day in which to receive them.
That is absolutely not correct.

Yes, I say the Roblin government have been showing extreme righteousness for the last two or three days or perhaps the last two or three months. I am dealing only with questions that arose during the time they had a free hand in the province of Manitoba to make voters' lists that were entirely in their own interest and denied the franchise to Liberals entitled to receive it. Applications must be made in person in Manitoba and there are numerous instances where men had to go one hundred miles to reach the registration booth. Let me quote from a speech of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford), who said :
I have here the name of one division where electors have to travel 400 miles to get their names on the list. In another division, if they had to make the return trip, they would have to travel 220 miles. In Swan River they would have to travel 145 miles each way.
These are illustrations to show that under the system of administration adopted by the Roblin government of Manitoba until a few weeks ago, every scheme imaginable was adopted in order to keep people oiff the voters' lists. who were entitled to go on them. It also occurred that the registration clerk could not complete his work in one day, and those who had not an opportunity to put their applications in remained disfranchised. These are some of the grievances complained of in the province of Manitoba.
My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) made some reference to British Columbia. Let me say at the outset that the people of British Columbia have never been educated down to doing small and mean things in connection with their election contests. The voters' lists have been honestly prepared. The people do not buy votes, they do not stuff ballot boxes, and they do not switch ballots ; and generally speaking, they play the game of politics fairly, as they play all other games. But while the voters' lists are honestly prepared, they offer the gravest possible encouragement for dishonesty. They are also loaded up with dead men and absentees. In each provincial

district there is a collector of votes who is generally the government agent or the mining recorder. He receives applications to be placed on the voters' list every day in the year. The applicant can get a blank form of declaration from any officer of the government, which he fills in and signs before a postmaster, alderman, mayor, justice of the peace or member of parliament, anybody in authority; and he hands in that application to the collector of votes. The application is placed on file, and twice in the year, in May and November, a court of revision is held. If there is no protest his name remains on the list. The operation of putting a man on the list in British Columbia is purely mechanical. No one ever thinks about anything crooked being done in having his name put on the list. There is a provision for getting names off the list not entitled to be there, but it is somewhat cumbersome and expensive. When there is a change in population, those lists often bear the names of absentees and others than bona fide voters. Let me give a personal illustration. A short time ago I sent out copies of a speech to the electors of my own district, using the latest revised voters' list, and through one post office alone nearly 200 of them came back endorsed by the postmaster, ' Left the country, present address unknown.' Then we have in British Columbia a large number of new men who are entitled to go on the voters' lists, and who can send in their application to the provincial collector of votes, but their names do not get on until the first court of revision in November. I propose to quote the opinion of a gentleman who took a very keen interest in public matters in British Columbia for a number of years, I refer to Mr. John Houston, who was president of the Conservative Association in British Columbia for a number of years. He was also a member of the local House. Mr. Houston is a Conservative, but sometimes he does not work at the game, and he is rather independent in the expression of his views. In his paper, the ' Empire,' published at Prince Rupert, he writes as follows :
British Columbia has a rotten system of registering votes, and there is no likelihood of the McBride government changing it for the better. Were the McBride government ousted from power, the Liberals would see to it that the law would be made even worse than it is.
Of course I cannot agree with that. What I am pointing out is that Mr. Houston is not a political partisan, though he was president of the Conservative Association of British Columbia ; and his criticism is directed against both parties.
Why, the reader will ask. Because neither the Conservative nor the Liberal parties in British Columbia have any desire to be fair to each other. The men who run the two parties are imbued with the idea that the people who vote have no rights that need be respected. Every voters' list in the province contains as many ' dead ' names as * live ' ones; and were the names of every person qualified to vote placed on the lists once a year, it is safe to assume that few of the men now members of the legislature would have M.P.P. added to their names. At the last provincial election in one district in Kootenay, 243 names were on the voters' list at one polling place; yet less than 50 votes were polled. The others were not in the district. At another polling place in the same district, over 100 men who had the qualifications of voters were not on the list because of the clumsy methods of registration. Yet Premier McBride and his attorney general will rage with fury because the Dominion government proposes to take a hand at revising lists that have been ' dead ' since 1903, and stuffed during the last six months.
Then lie makes suggestions as to how the lists should be prepared. Now here is an expression of opinion from an independent source to show that in the province of British Columbia, while I am prepared to adroit that the lists are prepared honestly, at the same time they are loaded up with dead men and with absentees.
Now what does this proposed legislation do ? As I understand the measure now before the House, it accepts the provincial lists as a basis for the federal lists. It provides for putting on the names of people who have been improperly left off, and it provides for striking off the names of people who should' not have been put on. In the preparation of the lists it provides for nothing that will in any way interfere or disturb the lists, honestly, efficiently and completely prepared by the provincial authorities ; or in other words, if the provincial authorities prepare honest lists, complete lists, there will be nothing to do for the Dominion officials appointed under this legislation.
Who are to be the judges whether the lists are honest or not ?
The judges appointed under this legislation.
They are government officials, I understand, appointed by this government.

What I mean to say is that the judges appointed under this legislation will put on or take names off the list in accordance with the laws of the province in which they are acting ; that is, they will supplement the work which the provincial authorities ought to have" done themselves ; and if the provincial authorities do their work properly there will be nothing for the Dominion revising judges to do. This Bill also provides the necessary authority to adjust the lists when there, is an overlapping of constituencies. My hon.

friend from Qu'Appelle, in answer to a question of mine the other night, suggested that there was no such authority in the old Act. Well, I think there was, but when our officials attempted to exercise that authority they were prosecuted by Colin Campbell, Attorney General of Manitoba.
In British Columbia, a portion of the provincial electoral district of Yale is in the New Westminster federal district and the other portion is in the federal district of Yale-Cariboo. The Yale-Cariboo election was a deferred election. The only list available was the provincial list for the whole provincial district of Yale. I may say to the House that in British Columbia we have no well defined polling subdivisions. I remember quite well that in the year 1901 neither one of the returning officers-the returning officer in New Westminster or the returning officer in Cariboo knew what to do with this list, but finally they decided that Armstrong, the New Westminster returning officer would guess at the people whom he thought should vote in New Westminster and he would vote those on November 1, while O'Hara, the returning officer in Yale-Cariboo, would vote the balance in Yale-Cariboo on November 22. The work was done the best way they * knew how and there was no complaint from either side because it was honestly done, but it afterwards developed that a small settlement south of Hope voted in New Westminster instead of Yale-Cariboo, and the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Kennedy) got a small Liberal majority to which I was entitled. The point I am making is that it is surely not arguable that there should not be some one in authority to furnish these returning officers with lists properly made and certified. It surely is not arguable that we should not have passed in this parliament such legislation as will put into the hands of returning officers lists upon which people may vote and not leave them open to prosecution at. the hands of partisan officials. I may say there was no trouble in British Columbia in 1904, because everybody thought the work was honestly done although it may have been imperfectly done. But, since then there has come to us in the province of British Columbia an attorney general who would indict His Majesty the King if he thought he could make any political capital out of it, and I for one do not propose that any officer of this government who is honestly attempting to do his duty in connection with an election should be open to prosecution or persecution at the hands of partisan officials of the provincial government.
Now. Sir, regarding the other clauses of the Bill, I have but little to say. I never had much confidence in legislation intended to make people honest in election time. I have very little patience with legislation Mr. D. ROSS.
that is intended as a sop to the Pharisee and which some of those who so loudly applaud have no intention of observing. I would put a man in jail for buying the elector.
I would put a man in jail for tampering with the ballot box or switching or mutilating ballots, and I think a man ought to go to jail for publishing absolutely false statements during an election campaign. But, I would not load up an election law with a lot of details which nobody intends to observe and which only bring the whole legislation into contempt and create a disregard for the bigger things that count.
A good deal has been said about the Liberal party going back on the position taken before 1896 and crystallized into legislation in 1898. Mr. Speaker, the principle of accepting provincial lists still remains, not-' withstanding the proposed amendments. Notwithstanding this legislation we still stick to the principle of accepting provincial voters' lists, and we do say that if these provincial voters' lists are honestly made there is nothing at all for any officer appointed under this proposed legislation to do. The amendments are intended to meet evils and defects that have arisen since the 1898 legislation became law. As I pointed out at the outset, the Solicitor General, who introduced that legislation, and the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who led the House at that time, stated that further legislation might be necessary to meet any evils that might arise in connection with the legislation then introduced.
Personally, I am not worried very much whether the Liberal party was theoretically right in 1898, or in any other year. I am satisfied it is right now. I am satisfied that this parliament should never divest itself of authority to ensure to the federal elector fully qualified his right to vote and notwithstanding anything that was said or done in 1898 or any other year, it would lie cowardice on our part not to pass legislation that will cure the existing evils despite the onslaughts on our opponents in this House and outside of it.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Ross) and while I do not desire to accuse that hon. gentleman of intentionally making statements that are not true, I will say that if the Manitoba Act was what the hon. gentleman says it is I would be the first man to vote against that Act and to substitute such a measure as I considered to be fair. There is not one Liberal member on the other side of the House from Manitoba who will say that the hon. gentleman's statements are true. I do not know whether he intended to go as far as he did in making those statements.

I made no comment whatsoever in regard to the Manitoba

Election Act; I made my comment with reference to the administration of the law.

I take the hon. gentleman's explanation and I say there is not a Liberal member on the other side of the House from Manitoba who will substantiate the statements that he made in connection with the administration of the law of that province. We have been discussing this question for a great many days and nearly every hon. gentleman from the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) down has devoted very little time to the question outside of the province of Manitoba. That little province, against which this government is doing all it can, has been occupying a great deal of the attention of this House during the last week. I stand here to-day, Mr. Speaker, asking for only a fair franchise Act. I believe it is the right of every citizen of this country to exercise his franchise and I am not one who will stand for any law, by whomever it may be made, that will disfranchise a man who is properly qualified to vote.
Let it be remembered that the present Dominion Franchise Act was passed in 1898 at a time when, X think I am safe in saying, all the provinces in the Dominion were administered by liberal governments. When the Liberals came to power the Franchise Act of 1885 was on the statute-book, and when they introduced their legislation in 1898 they had all those years between 1885 and 1898 to give it consideration and one would have thought that the Act they then passed would be the result of their best judgment and deliberation and knowledge. As I said, the provincial governments were then all Liberal and friendly to the Prime Minister. It is a fair question to ask the Prime Minister now : If there were Liberal governments in all the provinces to-day would we ever have heard of the Bill now before the House? I believe we would not. Surely if their Franchise Act of 1808 was good enough for the country then it ought to be good enough for the country to-day. I have a word to say with reference to the Minister of Justice. There is no man in this country who regrets more than I, that a gentleman like the Minister of Justice who has been so active in public life should be deprived of his hearing. It must be a great affliction to the hon. gentleman and I express personally my very great regret, but speaking for myself I do say it is hardly fair to this House and this country that such an important portfolio should be held by a gentleman who is absolutely unable to hear any argument that is presented after he delivers his address. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Rochel dealt with this question admirably and left little to be said and were it not that some hon. gentlemen on the other side from the province of Manitoba have made statements which are not supported by facts I doubt if I
would have taken part in the debate. Let me say again that as to the first clause in this Bill with which I am particularly concerned, my opinion is that the Minister of Justice had very little to do with it. My opinion is that the speech delivered by the hon. gentleman did not come from him, nor was it suggested by the Prime Minister of this country. I do believe it was suggested by the same man who suggested the Bill that was all printed and ready for introduction in 1904. The right hon. gentleman shakes his head. Does the right hon. gentleman mean that the Bill was not printed ?

All right, before we get through with this question we will see whether it was or not. I accept the right hon. gentleman's statement that a Bill was not printed but I do say that the father of this present Bill was the same gentleman who fathered the Bill in 1904. But the Bill of 1904 never was read even a first time in this House and I am going to give my version of why it was not read. I believe that the Minister of Justice of that day absolutely refused to have anything to do with it. I believe it is a logical conclusion to infer that the then Minister of Justice said : In 1898 we decided to adopt the franchise of the different provinces and I am not going to stand now for making an exception of that little province of Manitoba. That is the reason the Bill was dropped. I believe, Sir, that if the same hon. gentleman were Minister of Justice to-day the same fate would come to the Bill now before the House. That is my opinion any way. But the present Minister of Justice has not felt any difficulty apparently about introducing into this House a Bill that is most certainly designed to hit at the little postage stamp province of Manitoba. There have been rumours that a compromise would be arrived at if it was agreed that the Bill should be left applicable ta Manitoba and that the provisions with regard to British Columbia and the unorganized territories of Ontario and Quebec should be stricken out. 'Whether that is true or not I do not know but

it undoubtedly has been rumored. Now the first clause of this Bill says :
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary herein contained, voters' lists for the portions of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec which consist of territory not municipally organized and where there is no regular assessment or valuation roll upon which voters' lists are based, and for the several electoral districts in the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia shall be prepared immediately after the issue of any writ

Now, when I visited my people a short time ago I expressed my wonder to them why the province of Manitoba should be placed in exactly the same position as the unorganized backwoods of Ontario and Quebec. I wondered why it was that what was considered good enough for the backwoods should be considered good enough for Manitoba. I shall speak later about that provision for preparing the lists after the issue of tile writ. The section continues :
-after the issue of any writ for an election in any such electoral district or in any electoral district composed or partly composed of such territory, or at any time when the Governor in Council so directs.
Now, I have very little confidence in that reference to the governor in council. As a matter of fact we seldom know when an election is going to take place. Generally the first definite knowledge we have of an election is the issue of the writ so that the expression after the issue of the writ practically means nothing in its working out. I should think that taking it on the average the writ for an election is usually issued about four weeks before the election. Hon. gentlemen opposite have laid great stress on the point that under the Manitoba law there is not enough time given to prepare a fair list, but under the Manitoba Act there is two months given and I would like to know how this Bill is going to remedy that when as a matter of fact the machinery under it will only be set in motion after the issue of the writ which will give only four weeks for the preparation of the lists. Now, I do not think that the Minister of Justice gave a full or candid explanation of this Bill when he moved its second reading. He knew it was a contentious matter and that it had been condemned by the Conservative and independent newspapers of tlie country. I therefore have to complain that the explanation given by the Minister of Justice on such an important Bill was not such as it should be. I shall quote some of the remarks of the hon. gentleman and here is one statement of his :
In 1898 the present law was passed, the old Franchise Act of 1895 was repealed and the system of adopting the voters' lists prepared for the various provinces substituted in its stead. It was contended by different hon. gentlemen that whenever you have voters' lists prepared in the municipalities upon the basis Mr. SCHAFFNEE.
of the assessment roll you have to that extent a guarantee of substantiality and a guarantee of fairness.
Whether that be true or not I am not going to say, but the ' Globe,' the leading Liberal newspaper in the Dominion, took a very different view, and although the member for Lisgar stated the other day that the system of preparing the voters' lists was a fair one, I think I can show that in the past he expressed a very different view. The Minister of Justice continued :
The general outline of their system of preparing the voters' lists was that registration clerks were appionted for the various constituencies of the province.
I want to say that through all the speech of the Minister of Justice there is not more than a column that has reference to anything outside the province of Manitoba ; almost his who'e speech dealt with the thin red line and the province of Manitoba, and as his followers on the other side have followed the same line it is only fair to assume, as I said before that this Act was intended particularly to hit at Manitoba. I continue to quote from the Minister of Justice :
And the work of the registration clerks in forming the basis of the voters' lists was afterwards revised bv some member of a registration board, which consisted I think in practice of the county judges of the province, wrhich upon the face of the statute might consist either of the county judges or of barristers of three years standing.
Now, while that statement is partially correct, I do not think it is wholly correct, and I think the Minister of Justice was hardly fair in making it. As a matter of practice the revisions in Manitoba for the last few years have been made practically by the judges but the inference has been drawn by hon. members opposite that under the law of Manitoba the revision might be before a judge or a barrister of three years standing appointed by the government. That is not the fact and the Minister of Justice should have made his statement plainer. He should have said that the revision must take place before the judges or before revising barristers of three years standing appointed by these judges, and had he said that he would have told the [DOT]whole truth. The government of Manitoba have absolutely nothing to do with the appointing of those who are to revise the lists. It is the judge who revises the list in almost every instance, and if it is not the judge himself, the revision must be by a barrister whom the judge appoints. The government has no more to do with appointing these revising barristers than I have.
That is the present law ' of Manitoba.

That is the present law of Manitoba. I think I can also show that the very law which the hon. gentleman from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) advocated the other night is in great part the present law of Manitoba. The Minister of Justice continued to say :
The result is that throughout the whole province there is an overlapping. A Dominion constituency will have all round its borders an outstanding fringe consisting of portions of various surrounding provincial constituencies and in many instances the boundaries of the individual polling subdivisions in the provincial constituencies will not be coterminous with the boundaries of the Dominion constituency either.
The last part of the phrase is correct, but the first part is incorrect. I emphasize what I said before, that although hon. gentlemen opposite may not be disposed to accept any statements I may make, we on this side have the right to accent statements made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) in explaining so important a measure. We have the right to expect that any such statements will be absolutely founded on facts, and consequently ought to be accepted. Rut what do we find? We find the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) saying :
The result is that throughout the whole province there is an overlapping. A Dominion constituency will have all round its borders an outstanding fringe consisting of portions of .various surrounding provincial constituencies.
That statement is not correct. He went on to say :
Now, under the system of registration, as distinct from the system of preparing voters' lists with the assessment rolls as a basis, you have the voters' lists prepared for the various constituencies divided, not into polling subdivisions, but into registration districts, and the registration districts do not necessarily correspond with the polling subdivisions. They may or they may not do so, but the group of voters brought together by the registration check upon the one sheet of paper and certified to be qualified list of voters for a particular registration district consists, it may be, of men who vote in more than one polling subdivision.
Now, as a matter of fact, while it is not always the case that the registration districts correspond with the polling districts, I think that in the majority of cases they do, and that statement is not actually correct. In the majority of cases, in the majority of years, the registration districts absolutely correspond with the polling districts. I think I can safely make that statement, but you would gather from the language of the Minister of Justice that in very few cases they do. Further on, however, he makes a statement which rather contradicts that. He says :
The qualified list of voters for particular registration districts, consists, it may be, of men who vote in more than one polling subdivision.
Thai statement is misleading. A man cannot vote in more than one polling subdivision. It is a case of one man one vote. When a man has voted in one polling subdivision or electoral district, he cannot vote in another. Then the hon. minister goes on :
But more than that and worse than that, for the difficulty I am about to present, these voters are not in, I think I may safely say, the majority of instances, designated by. the ownership of a particular piece of property.
That is hardly a fair statement either. I can show here voters' list after voters' list made up in 1897, and there are very few in which there is not the name of the township, range, section, post office and occupation. Then the minister continued :
In some cases, possibly in the greater number of cases, the voters' post office .address is given, but in a groat many instances, in a very large percentage of the voters' lists throughout the country, not even a post office is (riven, but simply the name of the man entitled to vote.
If the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) were really aware of the facts, he would never expect any one in this House or out of it, who knew anything about the matter, to accept sucli a statement. The cases in which only the man's name is given, without any lots, section, range or post office are exceedingly rare, and the statement is not a fair one to make in connection with the lists. The hon. minister referred to a man named Anderson, living at Louise Bridge, occupation a mason, and he said:
That is the identification of the voter, and that is the case in respect of all the names throughout the list. The_vote>r's name, his post office and his occupation are given

lie made a different statement there :
-with no reference whatever to the property in respect of which he votes.
I call attention to that statement :
Or the exact place where he may live.
I want to tell the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) that a man does not vote m Manitoba in respect of any property. When the hon. minister made such a statement, either his intention must have been to mislead or he has never studied seriously the Manitoba Act and has been accepting blindly statements made to him by his hon. friends from that province. Here is the minister's statement :
With no reference whatever to the property in respect of which he votes.



But a man in Manitoba never votes in respect of property. There we have manhood suffrage. You are never asked whether you own any property or not.
Here comes a sentence, half a column in length, which I hope some one will be able to explain. It looks to me like a verification of the proverb that a drowning man catches at a straw. The Minister of Justice was trying to find some excuse why in 1908 this government should refuse to take the Manitoba Franchise Act-the very Act which they placed on the statute themselves. He was trying to find some excuse for going outside of that Act, and I propose to read the whole clause. I can make very little out of it:
I suppose it had not been thought of in 1898 or at any subsequent session of parliament. Possibly it was thought of in 1898 but considered not of practical importance for this reason: In 1898 the voters' lists in the province of Manitoba were not revised annually or at fixed times; they were revised whenever the Lieutenant Governor in Council so directed.
What innocent fellows they were in 1898! How little they were given to think what might happen in the future ! But I have no doubt the whole thing was well thought out. Let me go on quoting the hon. minister's remarks which will show clearly that they thought it out:
Accordingly the legislation of this parliament, as passed in 1898, provided that whenever that was the case with the voters' lists of any particular province, these voters' lists should not necessarily be accepted for the purpose of elections to this House. Our statute at the present time continues to provide that where, under the laws of any province, the voters' lists for any particular' electoral district or division are prepared, not at regular intervals, but at such times are fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, or by some other provincial or local authority, or only from time to time for the purpose of general or other elections in immediate contemplation, then the last preceding list shall be used, if it is less than a year old, but only in that event.
What the Minister of Justice, I think, was trying to point out was that surely they did not think they would be ever called upon to use the Manitoba lists. Well, granting that the province of Manitoba did not make out its lists more than once in four years, if there was an election once in three years, we would not have to use their lists, but we would any time in a year after they made up the lists. What I fail to see in his illustration is why we should not at all times adopt the lists made by the province of Manitoba.
If it is more than a year old the Dominion in that event prepares its own voters lists in the manner at present prescribed by the Dominion Elections Act and which has been on the statute-books since 1898. So that in 1898 Mr. SCBAFFNER.
when this legislation was passed repealing the old Franchise Act of 1885, Manitoba was not having annual revision of its lists, and was not in that sense affected by the Dominion legislation.
I say that in one year out of four it would be affected by the legislation of Manitoba.
But the provision of 1898, in the condition of things which then existed in Manitoba, was that the provincial lists of that province should be used for Dominion purposes only if there came a Dominion election when such lists were less than twelve months old, and that if such lists were at that time over twelve months old then the Dominion would prepare its own lists.
Now, he says :
That possibly is the explanation of the circumstance that no special provision was made in 1898 for the case of such overlapping as I have been describing.
Would not overlapping exist exactly the same in any way after the first year after the revision of the Manitoba lists? I say that argument is not clear nor is it a valid reason; it is not an argument that will appeal to members of this House or to the right hon. leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as a reason why in 1898 they did not foresee this state of affairs and why they are now introducing legislation trying to remedy it, The Minister of Justice went out of bis way to refer, if he will pardon me for saying it, in an undignified way for a man in bis position, to the manner in which we made up our lists. His language was more suited to the stump than to parliament. He said r
The Manitoba legislature provided by the statute of 1904, (repealing the provisions as to voters' lists which had theretofore existed in this province) that their registration should take place annually. It is true it was a sort of peculiar registration but it was what they called registration at all events.
I am prepared to prove to fair-minded men that we have not only ' a sort of registration,' but that we have a system of registration and a system of revision that for fairness and honesty and opportunity to Liberals and Conservatives alike to exercise their franchise is not excelled in any province. When the Minister of Justice sees fit to refer to our registration as a sort of registration be has failed to read and to be thoroughly seized of all that registration means in that country. He went on :
It was not registration preparing lists de novo by requiring each man who claimed the right to vote to appear before the official appointed for the purpose and state his claim, but it was the taking of the existing lists by the registration clerk and the adding to such lists or the i-evision of them on his part by making the changes which it might appear to be necessary. Accordingly we have the legislature of Manitoba ip the spring of 1904, by

the enactment I have referred to, making their provincial voters' lists revisable at regular annual intervals and no longer, at only such times as should be fixed by the government of the province. The effect was at once to make this provision of our Elections Act which authorized the Dominion authorities to prepare lists for the province of Manitoba no longer applicable to Manitoba.
I would like to know how he can justify that statement. He goes on to refer to the registration of 1903 as being made solely and entirely for the provincial elections. I take no exception to that statement, that was the duty of the officials. He proceeded:
Under these circumstances they were not prepared by the officials who were engaged in the work with any idea of their being used in Dominion elections.
What should they do? What was the point lie was trying to make? The duty of the provincial legislature was to make up a list for the provincial election and it is the duty of the Dominion government, according to their own laws, to take that list and use it for Dominion elections as they have always done.
They were not prepared in any way with reference to Dominion constituencies or Dominion polling subdivisions but with no other thought than the provincial limits I have mentioned.
I understand that this condition of affairs does not exist in Manitoba alone, that this overlapping, to which he must be referring here, exists in nearly every province. I know from reliable authority that it exists in Ontario, not only in the unorganized but also iu the organized parts which this Bill will not touch.
The Minister proceeded to speak of the size of some of the constituencies, and said :
We were investigating specially at that time the conditions with regard- to the three constituencies of Selkirk, Provencher and Macdonald and the size of these constituencies was stated to be in round figures: Selkirk, 100 miles wide by 210 miles in length; Provencher, 50 miles by 115 miles, and Macdonald, 80 miles by 86.
It could be proven that there are constituencies in this province just as large as that.
Suppose you had a constituency extending with regard to its width as far as from Toronto to Trenton, and so far as its length as far as from Toronto to Brockville, and you had a returning officer appointed for that whole territory, 100 miles one way and 210 miles in the other, and you place in his hands a series of voters' lists amounting to perhaps 4,000 or 5,000 voters in all, scattered over that territory, and with no other guide than at most the number of the lot and very probably with no other guide than the post office or possibly not even a post office, to enable 260J
him to say whether or not a particular voter is within these boundaries; why it is manifestly impossible that any man unless he has travelled from end to end of the province and from end to end of the constituency and unless he has a local knowledge greater far than the average citizen possesses, it is manifestly impossible that he would be able to do anything more than make one may say a guess, or secure such information as he could with reference to an individual and endeavour to make in that way lists which should he appropriate and legal for the purposes required.
That condition might exist in a very few outlying portions of Manitoba. Take the constituency of Selkirk. No doubt in the northern portion of that constituency there are some scattered voters, but when the hon. member for that constituency comes to speak I hope he will tell us how many people there are away up in the north and how many men have to travel 100 miles In order to register. There is no question that these cases are exceedingly exceptional.
The Minister of Justice, almost at the close of his speech, said :
I do not wish in the least to be misunderstood, and I assure you I am not in any degree blinking tbe situation, nor am I unwilling to take the fullest responsibility for the measure of redress as I believe this to be, which I am presenting to tbe House in the Bill now under consideration. Not only were there, in many instances throughout Manitoba the redistribution of names I have pointed out as absolutely requisite under this system of registration by registration districts, of these districts not corresponding to the boundaries of the Dominion constituency, but there was also a similar redistributing of names in oases where that was made requisite because of the Dominion returning officers subdividing polling divisions as they had existed for, provincial purposes.
Here the Minister of Justice makes a statement not in agreement with the statements, to which I have referred, in the earlier portion of his address.
In many cases, the registration districts of the province, which were supposed to correspond with the polling divisions, and which, I presume, in the main did correspond.
That is a fair statement.
The polling subdivisions in southern Manitoba practically correspond with the immigration districts. Then you may ask why call them registration districts? I think there is a very fair explanation, when yon are registering you are not polling, you register at a certain time, you poll at another time.
He does not say in every case. You would judge from the statement of the Minister of Justice to which I referred at the beginning, that they rarely if ever correspond ; but when he gets along this far he seems to have forgoten what he said

at first. He now says that they are supposed to correspond-' and which I presume in the main they did correspond ? '
Is that your opinion, that in the main they did correspond ?

That is my opinion, that in the majority of cases the polling subdivisions correspond with the registration districts. For instance, this year and many other years they absolutely correspond, I think that is the rule. I do not think the provision that the registration clerk shall he appointed from every polling subdivision, is carried out in every case, but that is the principle upon which they appoint their registration clerks.
_ Now, this is not a matter of political differences ; it is a matter of men entitled to vote being physically unable to record their votes between 9 and 5 o'clock on polling day, simply because they were too far distant from the pole to make the journey. . . In the whole province, I suppose, there is a matter of 50,000 names to be handled upon the voters' lists. I think, if you have 10 returning officers sent down with 50,000 names, 5,000 on the average for each one to distribute according to their proper polling subdivisions, to do that work in the four weeks that pass between the receipt of the writ and the re-ceint of these lists, and the polling day, to get together the necessary information and do the best they can-
1 think I have proved that about four weeks was all that the Minister of Justice was going to give to do this work, and if It is impossible to do it in the four weeks, why is it impossible to do it In about six weeks given by the provincial government? It is about two months from the time the machinery starts until polling day. Then he goes on :
That that should take place, you have a condition of things that calls for a change, and calls for legislation in this parliament which would make it impossible, so far as human foresight can do so, that the same state of things should occur again; and that is the whole purpose of the legislation in question so far as this provision of it is concerned.
And further on :
Whatever the reason, the result has been that the time allowed for the revision in each year since then has been, according to the view at any rate of the one political party, entirely inadequate for the purpose. The statute requires notices of appeal from the registration clerk to he given within a certain number of days from the closing of the work of the registration clerk. The statute empowers the Lieutentant Governor in Council to fix the number of days upon which the revising officer, judge or barrister shall sit on his work, and when the day fixed by the proclamation for the concluding of that hearing of appeals or revising work is passed, there is no power on the part of the officer to continue his work, no matter how much may re-Mr. SCHAFFNER.
main to be done and no matter how many appeals may remain unheard.
Now it does seem to me that this Act gives the revising officer, who, is the judge, the power mentioned by the Minister of Justice in this statement. I will read clause 61 of the Manitoba Act :
In order to give full and due effect to the powers of the board, the said board may provide for any proceeding, matter or thing for which express provision has not been herein made, or for which only partial provision has been made; or, where it shall be found that the time allowed to do any act is insufficient and an alteration or extension of such time, and any alteration of dates consequent thereon, shall appear to lie necessary, the board may declare that such alteration shall be made, and thereupon the same shall be made and take effect accordingly.
Not being a lawyer, it seems to me that gives the revising officer, who is the judge, the power, if he thinks there is not sufficient time for the revision at any particular place, to extend the time. I would like the First Minister, if he has not examined that clause, to look into it.
What is the date of the Act ?

1904, revised to 1900. If that has been changed, I am not aware of it, but I do not think that clause has been repealed :
It is alleged that such men are of one political party, that their names are left off right and left by the registration clerks, that their only means of getting on the list and obtaining the right to exercise their franchise is by appeal to the judge, and that the judge is given, it may be for a whole constituency, but one day between the hours of ten and- five within which to do the work of days or weeks.
That is an unfair statement, I do not care who makes it. A challenge has been thrown out by a Winnipeg paper, which covers past time, that $25 will be paid for every man our adversaries can find who, being a legally qualified voter, has presented himself to the registration clerk in Manitoba and has been refused the right to have his name put on the list. That challenge has been printed and sent abroad, and I intend to quote it before I am through. Now the Minister of Justice was not making a fair statement when he said that these men are of one political party and their names are left off right and left. I make the statement that the Liberals in the province of Manitoba, and I challenge contradiction, have absolutely the same opportunity and the same privilege of getting on the voters' lists as the'Conservatives. When the Minister of Justice says that the judge has only one day between the hours of 10 and 5 to do the work, he is in error, perhaps it is a clerical error, because the actual time is from 11 to 6. However, that shows

what I have been trying to prove, that the Minister of Justice did not make himself very familiar with the Manitoba Act before he attempted to discuss it, when he introduced this Bill on the 9th of March. He says :
In the constituencies of Kildonan and St. Andrew's-
That may be an error of ' Hansard,' because Kildonan and St. Andrew's are all in one constituency.
But without questioning what the merits or demerits of the provincial system may be, I say that it is manifest that any system, no matter how good, may he administered that it will be oppressive and unjust, and that there is at any rate ground for complaint that the present system in Manitoba as at present administered in the preparation of the voters' lists, is an engine of tyranny

That is the definition given by the Minister of Justice to this House of an .Act in the province of Manitoba which can be absolutely proven to be fair.
-and oppression as against the party that is opposed to the provincial government.
That is a statement which is absolutely unfair, to say the least.
In the condition which now exists in Manitoba, with voters' lists which were prepared more than five years ago, with voters' lists that have never been since that time effectively revised, with voters' lists therefore that contain the names of hundreds of men who are either dead or departed from the province, we have lists that need revision.
The man on the street would infer from the remarks of the hon. Minister of Justice that since 1904 we had never had a revision of the lists when, as a matter of fact, every year the names of dead men and absentees are taken from the list, the lists are verified and the names of men who have come of age or who have come to the province during the year are added to the list. Is it any wonder, after reading over the remarks of the Minister of Justice, that I 'made the statement which I did at the beginning of my speech ?
We have lists that ought to be submitted to the work of a revising officer, a county judge or a barrister according to the Manitoba system, with time given him within which he can effectively do that work

Will the Prime Minister tell me how he is going to get time to do that work if he has not time now ? He is going to begin to put the machinery in operation after the issuing of the writ, and if so it is absolutely impossible for him to do that work and the Minister of Justice failed to explain that when stating the objects of his Bill.
-of revision, within which he can effectively purge the lists of dead men and of absentees, the presence of which upon these lists is but
an invitation and a temptation to impersonation.
I suppose there has never been any impersonation going on in the province of Ontario. I am not going to refer to that to-day, but I think we have very good evidence that the impersonation has not all been in the province of Manitoba.
We have lists from which the names of hundreds of men in Manitoba are absent-hun-di eds of men who, whether rightly or wrongly. claim the right to be upon those lists, and the right to exercise their franchise; men who claim at any rate that they have been prevented from having their claims adjudicated by the insufficiency of the time allowed under the statute for the purpose of revision.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these are all the remarks that I have to make in connection with the speech of the Minister of Justice.
I have tried to be fair. I have read his words and, in finishing my references to the Minister of Justice, I repeat the statement that I made at the outset, that his remarks were very unfair. They were unfair to his own people. The members on the other side of the House had a right to expect a fair definition of this Bill from the Minister of Justice, and I have tried to prove that his statements are not statements that can be borne out by the facts.	*

When the House rose at six o'clock, I had finished dealing with what I believe to have been the unfair exposition made by the Minister of Justice of the provisions of the Manitoba Franchise Act. Let me point out that when this government saw fit to make a new franchise Act in 1898, they found the boundaries of the federal districts coterminous with those of the provincial districts all over Canada. It has been argued by gentlemen on the other side that this condi-f tion does not exist to-day. But if it does not exist it is because this present federal government changed the boundaries of the federal electoral districts, and it is they who are to blame. The great underlying principle of the Manitoba Franchise Act of 1903, was a personal registration. The present Manitoba government was impressed with the fact that personal registration was the fairest way to compile a voters' list and so they adopted that principle. They came to power in 1899, but they did not change the Election Act until 1903. One of the members spoke the other night about bloodshed and I do not know what he meant by that, but I do say that so far as I am concerned, after the 27th of June I will be staying here at as great a sacrifice as any member of this House, but I am prepared to make that sacrifice. The Conservative members of Manitoba are standing for a principle which they are prepared to defend to the last, and I believe that we, as well as every member on this side of the House, are determined to resort to every constitutional and legitimate means to prevent this Bill becoming the law of Canada.

I do not intend to detain the House at any great length but I feel it incumbent on me to reply to some of the remarks addressed to the House by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche). At page 8270 of ' Hansard '

he refers to the difficulties that the Conservatives had in Manitoba in the year 1899 In trying to clean up the electoral lists preparatory to a provincial election ; but I think it would be interesting for him to know the troubles we had in my own constituency in 1906 in trying to purge the lists of that year. The hon. member for Souris has been telling us for the last three hours about certain happenings in Manitoba and amongst other things he said that in 1899 it cost the Conservatives about $30,000 to clean up the provincial lists. Perhaps it may astonish him when I tell him that when we'undertook to do some cleaning of the provincial lists previous to the last provincial election it cost us in my own county about one-tenth of the sum he named, and the results I think will be surprising to him. In the local division of Kockwood we added 102 names and struck off 264 or a total of 366.
In Gimli we added 81 and struck off 45 ; in Springfield we added 160 and struck off 111 ; in Kildonan and St. Andrews we added 122 and struck off 127; total for the four constituencies, 1,012; average for each constituency, 253. The Conservative changes in 1899 for 40 constituencies were 7,371, an average for each constituency of 1844, or 68J less changes in each constituency than we had in 1906. Any hon. gentleman can verify that from the voters' lists which I have'here and which I will lay on the table of the House. I leave in for the purpose of this comparison the three Winnipeg constituencies. If we took these out the comparison would show much more to the advantage of the Greenway Act. Therefore,I think it will be fair for us to say that that much-abused Act was certainly a very favourable Act compared with the Act we now have on the statute-book. As far as I am concerned, I have not very much objection to the present Act in Manitoba ; it is not the Act itself that I have objection to, but the administration of it by order in council. There is nothing stable about the Act; we do not know from year to year what we may expect. In the last six years every year they have given us something different from what we have had every other year, so that we do not know what to expect. We hear to-day that a new proclamation has been issued-they are going to give us more time for revision. This just goes to show why this Knatter should be in the hands of the Dominion authorities. I do not want it to be in the hands of partisans on the other side, because I know what we have been treated to in the past.
Do you want partisans on your own side?
No, I do not want that. In my speech in 1905 I said that if we had a Municipal Act such as they have in the province of Ontario, I would be satisfied.

I am not speaking of what Mr. Greenway said ; I am speaking for myself.
The hon. gentleman wras supporting Mr. Greenway in the legislature at the time.

Yes, and I have nothing to regret in the support I gave that hon. gentleman for twelve years. We had the best government in Manitoba then that we have ever had. I will just show you, by a table I have here, the difference between this Act and the Greenway Act as to the time given for registration. In 1903 they gave 1,980 days; in 1904, 347 days ; in 1905, 40 days ; in 1908 they are giving us 392 days. I have not the figures for 1906 and 1907, but they were different from every one of these others. Every year since 1903 we have had a different basis ; we do not know what to expect, because the law is not a law on the statute-book, but a law by order in council-that is the objection I have to it.

In my opinion' there is no comparison between the two Acts. The only objection raised against the Greenway Act was as to enumerators. a difficulty in a voter getting on by application. I think there might possibly be found one of the men they have now appointed as registration clerks that will perhaps not be just the fair thing. That is all I have to say now, so far as Mr. Greenway's Act is concerned.

Chas. Mickle regarding the Act. Let me just quote-wliat the Hon. Charles Mickle said when the amendment to the 1902 Act was being moved in 1904. In resuming the debate on tlie Election Act, lie said :
In resuming the debate on the Election Act amendments Mr. Mickle stated that it was usual in such cases for the government to give some explanations, not merely as to why a new measure was introduced, but also for any new departure from principles heretofore accepted and acted upon. The Bill before the House involved radical departures from established precedent and from the policy the government had before pursued; but no explanations had heen offered by the attorney general in his speech on the reason for those departures. The essence of the existing election law was the principle of personal registration, and in the amending law that principle had heen abandoned. From the beginning to the end of the attorney general s address there had heen no explanation ot this abandonment. True, he had gone over the amending clauses w-ith some care and particularity, but no explanation or defence of the new principles involved in the Bill had been forthcoming.	.
One thing, however, was very plain, and must lie admitted by everyone who examined the Bill-that in substance it w-as a capitulation Oil the part of the government to the soundness of the principles for which the Liberal party in Manitoba had long contended.
Mr. Mickle stated that in the past few years there had been some important changes in the Franchise Act of the province. The 1 ran-chise Act of the Greemvay government had been based on th/i municipal lists. When this government came to power they found fault with this principle and succeeded in getting a new principle adopted which had now heen in force some years.	.
In defence of the principles underlying the present Franchise Act, much might be saul. Three main features were embodied in the present law-personal registration, the placing the making of the voters' lists in the hands of the judges, and the educational test. The new law did away with some of the most objectionable features of the old. Some of the Liberals had taken exception to the principle of personal registration, as being inconvenient, troublesome and cumbersome. These objections -were now removed, for the principle the government introduced and fought for had entirely disappeared. The new Act provided that the list, with annual alterations, should exist for the next twenty or thirty years. The principle of personal registration, as Mr. I Mickle understood it, implied personal registration for the preparation of every list.



Prom this principle and practice the new Act was an entire departure.
Another advantage claimed under the present Act was that the making of the lists was taken out of the hands of partisan officials and put in the hands of the judges. This provision, also, was wiped out by the proposed legislation. It was reasonable and fairly satisfactory in practice under the present Act, but now it was done away with. Henceforth the registration clerks were to be appointed by the government. True, there was still a board of registration, but it was not for the receiving of names but for the appointment of revising officers. If the principle adopted under the present Act had the merits claimed, what reason was there for the changes now sought to be introduced?
Regarding the third principle in the present law, that the voters' lists should be prepared for each general election, Mr. Mickle said that by this means the public was apprised of the approaching contest, and took the necessary interest therein to register. But the new Act provides for annual lists, whether or not an election was impending. The inevitable result would be that three years out of the four, the apathy of the electors would make the so-called revision useless.
Mr. Mickle then went on to point out that the Act was vague in many important respects. As he understood it, there was to be only one place in each electoral division for registering. In many of the larger constituencies this would impose much hardship on those desirous of registering. This provision he disapproved. The hours of registration, and the number of days were not specified.
I think that when the hon. member for Marquette appeals to the right hon. First Minister to take cognizance of the opinion of Mr. Mickle, it was not this opinion he wished the right hon. gentleman to follow.

The Revised Statutes of Manitoba, vol-umn 1, 1902, page 859, clause 47, provides that the registration clerk shall enter on his register the name, occupation and residence of applicants. There does not appear to be any post offices required by this clause to be put after qualification of voters, but we find that in the Statutes of Manitoba, assented to on the 8th day of February, 1904, page 27, section 15, also the Manitoba Elections' Act, 1904, chapter 52, page 10, section 31 provides for the post office being put after the qualification of voters. One .of two words with regard to Manitoba. It is proposed in order to put these men on the lists to send out an enumerator. Is he going to be qualified as a valuator in order that he shall determine whether a certain farmer should be put on the list, whether his property is sufficient to entitle him to go on the list, whether if he has one or more sons the property is valuable enough to entitle them all to a vote. And affer the enumerator has traversed the riding and made his lists, it would be utterly impossible to have an appeal to any judge because 30 days would have expired and then the decision of this enumerator would be final. It has always been deemed wise to have an appeal to a judge in such cases. Is an exception going to be made here? If the appeal is cut out, injustice and wrong may follow. Looked at from every standpoint, I fear that this clause 9A has been conceived in iniquity and born in sin, if it ever comes to birth. Now, the province of Quebec has been in the hands of friends of the Prime Minister for a good many years and if there is any crying grievance in that province, surely the remedy can easily be applied. Our friends on the opposite side cannot claim that they have an unfriendly government in the province of Quebec. has to do in the province of Quebec is to say to one: Go, and he goeth and to another: Come, and he cometh. He said that they had not descended to the bickerings which people apparently did in other parts of the country, and that the voters' list was honestly compiled and everybody entitled to a vote was put on it. If this government were taking hold or this question from the broad standpoint of making a voters' list for the whole Dominion, I would give it my support. It does seem to be an anomaly that we should have all kinds of qualifications, people voting half a dozen times in one province and only once in another. There are many reasons why we should have a uniform Franchise Act covering the whole Dominion. But this Bill does not attempt to touch any grievance. Its effect will be to perpetuate any thing evil in the present situation, rather than to remedy it. Looking at the Bill from every standpoint, I cannot see any good reason for it. and after being properly advertised, so that everybody would have an opportunity of knowing that he was on the voters' list and that somebody was appealing to have his name knocked off, or of having his name put on if it is not there. This is all that I intend to say on this question. I followed this debate with much interest. I am satisfied that grave injustices has been made in the province of Manitoba. In the Bill before us, I see a remedy to this, and I cannot do otherwise than to support it in principle.
I have no doubt that when the Bill will come in committee, that amendments will be made. In these circumstances I am proud to give to the Bill my hearty support.
